text: Mansplaining Feminism, wave one, part two. Last time we stopped around 1830 when it seemed that it was over for feminism. The founding voices were gone. The laws had moved backwards under Napoleon. The culture had closed in around the idea that a woman's place was at home. On paper, the whole thing just looked finished. But it wasn't, because while the woman question looked buried, something was quietly keeping it alive. And it came from a place almost nobody expected, the movement to end slavery. You see, through the 1820s and 30s, the movement to end slavery was spreading across Britain and the United States, and women poured into it. But how was that even possible? Didn't that era have a strict rule? A woman's place was the home, not public life? Well, there was a loophole. You see, women were also cast as the moral guardians of society, and slavery was framed as a moral evil. So fighting it wasn't politics, it was morality, which meant women were allowed in. It was one of the few public causes a respectable woman could join without a scandal. So they did, by the thousands. They organized, they wrote, they raised money, they gathered signatures. And in the process, they learned how to build a movement from the ground up. And somewhere in that work, a quiet realization started to spread. We are fighting for the freedom of other people, which is great, but there are also rights we don't have ourselves. The clearest example, the Grimke sisters, Sarah and Angelina. Two southern women, daughters of a slaveholder, who turned against slavery and became star speakers for the cause in the 1830s. And that's where they crossed the line. Women were welcome in the movement, quietly, organizing, writing, raising money. The Grimkes stood on a stage and spoke to crowds, that included men. A woman addressing men with authority, that was the real taboo, and they broke it. The backlash was fast, led by the clergy. Their claim was simple, it's unnatural for a woman to speak this way. God gave her a smaller, quieter place. In 1838, Sarah answered, that isn't God talking, she argued, it's men defending their own advantage, and calling it the natural order. In her own words, take their feet from off our necks. And notice what just happened. A woman fighting for someone else's freedom had been forced to start arguing for her own. The connection was now out in the open, and it couldn't be unseen. Then came the moment that lit the fuse. London, 1840. A huge world anti-slavery convention. A group of Americans sailed over to attend, among them Lucretia Mott, a delegate, and a young woman named Elizabeth Cady Stanton. They're alongside her abolitionist husband. But when they arrive, the convention takes a vote, and decides, the women aren't allowed to participate. They're sent up to a curtain of gallery, allowed to watch, but not take part. Think about that, a gathering devoted to human freedom, that wouldn't let women take a seat. So Mott and Stanton, side by side behind that curtain, start talking. And out of that humiliation comes an idea. If we want this to change, we have to organize for ourselves. But they don't. They go home. They live far apart. Stanton disappears into raising a house full of children. Mott has her own work, her own causes. And the idea from London just sits there, for 8 years. Then, in the summer of 1848, Mott is visiting upstate New York. And Stanton, along with a couple of other ladies, comes to see her over tea. No agenda, just a social afternoon. But Stanton had been holding a lot in. She'd been part of the abolition world once. The arguments, the organizing, the feeling of fighting for something that mattered. And then, it had narrowed to a household in a small town, far from the movement she'd once belonged to. She couldn't vote, and as a married woman, the law treated her property, her wages, even her contract as her husband's, not her own. And the women around the table understood it instantly. Because it wasn't just Stanton. It was the position of women more broadly. A whole half of the population with no real voice in the laws they lived under, and no organized way to even object. That was the shift. This wasn't a private complaint. It was a problem you could organize against. The same way they'd learned to organize for abolition. So right there, over tea, they made that decision. Enough waiting. Let's hold a convention.
